source_text: Hoc quoque die ob passionem Domini Jesu Christi aut stationem Deo, aut jejunium, facimus. Die septimo requievit ab omnibus operibus suis, et benedixit eum et sanctificavit. Hoc die solemus superponere; idcirco, ut die Dominico cum gratiarum actione ad panem exeamus. Et parasceve superpositio fiat, ne quid cum Judaeis sabbatum observare videamur, quod ipse Dominus sabbati Christus per prophetas suos odisse animam suam dicit (Is., I, 13, 14); quod sabbato corpore suo resolvit: prius autem, cum ipse Moysi praeciperet, ne circumcisio diem octavum praeteriret, quae die sabbato plerumque incurrit, sicut in evangelio scriptum legimus (Joan., VII, 22). Moyses prospiciens duritiam populi illius (Mat., XIX, 8), idcirco die sabbati legebamus (Ex., XVII, 9, 12; Col., II, 14), et seipsum crucifixit. Et praelio quae, ab allophylis sabbato (I Mac., II, 31--41), ut caperentur, et velut severitatem legis ad devetando disciplinam formarentur.
pass_a_gloss: On parasceve: station/jejunium for Christ's passion. Die septimo God rested/blessed; Christians superpose so die Dominico they go ad panem with thanksgiving. Avoid sabbath-with-Jews—Christus Dominus sabbati hates it (Isa 1); dissolved it in His body; circumcision on 8th day can fall on sabbath.
pass_b_english: On this day also, because of the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, we keep either a station to God or a fast. On the seventh day He rested from all His works, and blessed it and sanctified it. On this day we are accustomed to make a carrying-over, so that on the Lord's Day we may go forth to the bread with thanksgiving. And let a carrying-over be made from the parasceve, lest we seem to keep the Sabbath with the Jews in any way—which Sabbath the Lord of the Sabbath, Christ, says through His prophets that His soul hates (Isa. 1:13–14); which Sabbath He dissolved in His own body. Earlier, when He Himself commanded Moses that circumcision not pass beyond the eighth day, which often falls on a Sabbath day, as we read written in the Gospel (John 7:22). Moses, foreseeing the hardness of that people (Matt. 19:8), therefore on the Sabbath day—we used to read (Ex. 17:9, 12; Col. 2:14)—also crucified the ordinance itself. And there were battles which, from the foreigners on the Sabbath (1 Macc. 2:31–41), so that they might be captured, and as it were the severity of the law might be shaped toward avoiding a discipline.
